growth_story.headline: Sri Lanka's post-war boom gave way to tax cuts, shocks and a 2022 default; income per person has recovered but is still below its 2018 peak.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2002, during a long internal conflict, income per person grew 3.1 percent a year, with a fall of 3.1 percent in 2001. Growth rose to 5.6 percent a year from 2003 to 2017, and the World Bank says much of the boom after the conflict ended in 2009 came from public investment to rebuild, led by construction, transport and other sectors that do not sell abroad. Since 2018 growth has averaged 0.1 percent a year: the IMF says the Easter Sunday attacks and large tax cuts in 2019 left the country exposed, and it lost access to foreign bond markets when the pandemic hit. In 2022 reserves ran out, the country stopped paying its external debt, and income per person fell 7.5 percent. With budget repair, exchange rate reform and debt restructuring under an IMF program, income per person grew 5.6 percent in 2024 and 5.7 percent in 2025. Even so, in 2025 it was still 1.2 percent below its 2018 peak, about where it first was in 2017, and the last decade averaged 1.0 percent a year against 6.0 in the decade before.

threads.title: Peace and a building boom
threads.text: The end of the internal conflict in 2009 brought what the World Bank called a peace dividend, and growth sped up. Much of it came from public investment to rebuild, and the sectors that grew most were construction, transport, domestic trade, and banking, insurance and real estate, none of which sell abroad. Income per person grew 5.6 percent a year from 2003 to 2017.

threads.title: Attacks, tax cuts and pandemic
threads.text: Before the pandemic the country already had thin reserves and risky public debt. The IMF says the Easter Sunday attacks and large tax cuts in late 2019 made this worse, and when the pandemic hit Sri Lanka lost access to foreign bond markets. Income per person fell 0.8 percent in 2019 and 5.1 percent in 2020.

threads.text: After years of budget deficits and unsustainable debt, depleted reserves caused severe shortages of fuel, food and medicine in 2022, and in April the country stopped paying its external debt. Income per person fell 7.5 percent in 2022 and another 1.4 percent in 2023.

threads.title: Recovery after restructuring
threads.text: Budget repair, exchange rate reform and debt restructuring under an IMF program brought growth back, and income per person rose 5.6 percent in 2024 and 5.7 percent in 2025. The recovery is still incomplete: poverty remains high, and investment fell from 31.6 percent of GDP in 2017 to 18.2 in 2023 before rising to 20.8 in 2025. The IMF says private business and foreign investment are still well below their potential.

growth_story.tension: In October 2026 the World Bank said real GDP is back at pre-crisis levels, a year after saying output was still below 2018 levels. The data show income per person in 2025 still 1.2 percent below its 2018 peak, about where it first was in 2017. The data also show income per person growing 5.6 percent in 2024 and 5.7 percent in 2025, faster than the World Bank's growth estimates for the whole economy. That would mean a shrinking population, or that the two data releases differ.
